summary:
Same-sex sexual activity is criminal in Comoros. Article 300 of the 2020 Penal Code punishes any act of a sexual nature contrary to morality or unnatural, and the sources in this record disagree on the penalty. Outright International, and the text of Article 300 as quoted in reference material, give six months to two years imprisonment plus a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs, about US$240 to US$720. An archived copy of the 2020 Penal Code specifies two to five years and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs. Human Dignity Trust records a maximum of three years. A December 2024 press report on the Comoros court cites Article 318 as the operative provision, carrying up to five years.

The 1982 Penal Code that preceded the current statute punished the same conduct with up to five years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 1,000,000 francs.

Enforcement is documented. In 2022 a man was prosecuted after a sexual video of him with another man was leaked online, recorded as the first prosecution of consensual adult same-sex activity under the 2020 Penal Code. In June 2024 two women were arrested after asking an imam to marry them; the request was not proven in court, but the women stated they had previously had sexual relations. They were detained from June until December 2024, convicted of homosexuality on 12 December 2024, and sentenced to five and six months respectively, then released because the terms were shorter than the time already served. Reuters and the Washington Blade both reported the December 2024 ruling, and Human Dignity Trust called the conviction a human-rights violation. The most recent documented enforcement case in this record is the December 2024 conviction; no later instance is documented.

The US State Department's 2023 human rights report on Comoros states that authorities reported no arrests or prosecutions for same-sex conduct during 2023 and did not actively enforce the criminalising law that year. The same report records that police stated they did not incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons and that none was reported in 2023, while listing widespread impunity among the country's major human-rights problems. No non-discrimination law exists.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable: transgender people are not permitted to change their gender markers, and no law prohibits discrimination based on gender identity. The 2012 Labor Code provides no protection for LGBTQ people.

There is no recognition of legal rights for couples read as same-sex. The Family Code defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman.

The government has repeatedly declined to decriminalise homosexuality when recommended by United Nations bodies. No LGBTIQ organisation is known to operate in the country; Article 5 of Law No. 86-006/AF of 1986 prohibits organisations founded on an unlawful cause or for an unlawful purpose contrary to the law or public morals, which reference material identifies as chilling registration of such groups.
tangentialFactors:
Societal climate bears on visibility rather than on statute. Reference material records stigmatisation of LGBTQ people in the broader population, discrimination in education and employment, and ostracism from homes, neighbourhoods and villages; it states that most LGBTQ people did not disclose their sexual orientation or gender identity as of 2023. That material offers no documented statement about societal treatment of transgender people specifically.

A 2023 Gallup poll of residents asked whether their area was a good place for LGBTQ people, with 26 percent answering yes, ten percentage points above the previous year. The survey measured views about LGBTQ people generally, not about transgender people, and it describes resident opinion rather than visitor exposure.

The penalty attached to the criminalising provision is reported four different ways across the sources in this record, ranging from a six-month minimum to a five-year maximum, and the article number is given as both 300 and 318. A visitor cannot determine from these sources which sentence a Comoran court would impose.

Enforcement in this record is episodic and case-driven: a leaked video in 2022, and a marriage request to an imam in 2024, rather than systematic policing. The 2023 reporting year saw no arrests or prosecutions at all.
localsOnly:
Residents have no legal route to change a gender marker, and no statute bars discrimination on the basis of gender identity. The 2012 Labor Code offers LGBTQ workers no protection.

Marriage under the Family Code is the union of a man and a woman, so couples read as same-sex have no legal standing as partners, with no inheritance, hospital-visitation or next-of-kin recognition documented in this record.

Organising is obstructed: Article 5 of Law No. 86-006/AF of 1986 allows prosecution of organisations formed for purposes contrary to law or public morals, and no LGBTIQ organisation is known to exist in Comoros. Outright International records this provision as the reason registration is not attempted.

Residents accused under the provision face the penalty dispute described above, and the two women held from June to December 2024 served five and six month sentences in full before release. The government has repeatedly refused United Nations recommendations to decriminalise the conduct.

Non-disclosure was the reported norm among LGBTQ residents as of 2023, alongside documented discrimination in schooling and work and ostracism from family and community.
outOfScopeNotes:
The penalty for the criminalising offence is unresolved in this record: four sources give four ranges and two different article numbers. No source consulted here reconciles them or states which text is currently in force in the courts.

No source in this inventory addresses entry or visa rules for transgender travellers, passport or marker requirements at Comoran border control, airport screening treatment of gender-nonconforming travellers, access to hormone therapy or trans-related healthcare, or availability of gendered facilities. These areas are not sourced rather than assessed.

The inventory contains no documented incident of violence against a trans person in Comoros and no trans-specific violence statistics. The most recent documented enforcement action against same-sex conduct is the 12 December 2024 conviction.

The US State Department's 2010 human rights report on Comoros records only limited content on LGBT issues and is not used here; its material on prison conditions, movement, press, religion and women's discrimination does not bear on trans visitor risk.
